To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sarcolemma is detached from myofibril in both normal and callipygous lamb during postmortem aging, but the detachment is delayed in callipyge.
postmortem storage does not affect (0% to 3%) myofibril stability in callipyge, but it increases the percentage of I-band break in the normal longissimus from 0 to 11%.
the major factor that makes the meat of callipyge lambs tough is the postmortemp stability of myofibers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ultrastructural changes in postmortem normal and callipygee longissimus.
the ultrastructural changes of myofibrillar proteins in postmortem normal and callipygeness longissimus.
the mechanism by which callipyge causes meat to be tougher than normal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the callipyge mutation affects the postmortem tendering of muscle in the longissimus by delaying the loss of lateral attachments of myofibrillar proteins and the I-band break.

the callipyge gene is responsible for a major increase in postmortem stability in the longissimus dorsi muscle, and that postmortem stability is a major factor responsible for toughness of meat from the longissimus of callipyge lamb.
postmortem stability and toughness of the myofibril are the major factors that determine meat tenderness in callipyge lamb.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the callipyge phenotype is characterized by a unique ultrastructural organization in the endomysial region of the longissimus muscle.

the major factor for postmortem stability is the stability of the I-band region of the myofibril, and the stability of the myofibers and sarcolemma is not the major factor for the postmortem tenderation.
the postmortem tenderizing process is delayed in callipyge muscle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sarcolemma does not seem to contribute significantly to the tenderization of meat during postmortem aging.
the callipyge mutation is associated with the stability of the myofibrils, which is the primary determinant of postmortem tenderness.
postmortem tenderizing mechanisms are different in callipyge and normal muscle.
